body:
The MRP has some extra code in it beyond what is used to cause the issue, but even after removing some of this the issue is still reproducible for me on 4.7.stable, though moving the window doesn't always seem to cause a physics update for me. It's possible there is still some code that is causing the issue which I didn't identify.

Various interaction sets reproduce the issue after an inconsistent amount of time:
- Moving just one letter repeatedly until the issue occurs
- Alternating between which letter is moved until the issue occurs
- Moving one letter just once, waiting briefly, and then encountering the issue

I tried waiting for over 60 seconds after launching the project (usually the issue occurs by this point when interacting), but I was still able to get an interaction or two in before it locks up. Sometimes one envelope will lock up while the other is still interactable, this seems to happen when one is moving but the other is not (stationary one is locked, moving one is not).

```
Godot v4.7.stable - macOS Tahoe (26.5.1) - Multi-window, 1 monitor - Metal (Forward+) - integrated Apple M1 (Apple7) - Apple M1 (8 threads) - 16.00 GiB memory - CoreAudio (48000 Hz, Stereo/mono)
```

I have reproduced this and can confirm the issue.

Your MRP works fine with 4.6.3-stable.

If I then cherry-pickCommit f6da6bf on top of 4.6.3-stable, then it breaks. From this pull request:
[Only propagate physics server transforms when different #118080](https://github.com/godotengine/godot/pull/118080)

This is effectively a duplicate of #121038, except in this case the `RigidBody2D` in question (`physical_letter` and `physical_letter2`) aren't having their transforms modified directly, but instead indirectly through their parent's transform being continuously modified here:

```gdscript
func _process(delta: float) -> void:
	
	var view :Vector2= get_viewport_rect().size
	#print(get_viewport_rect())
	position = view / 2
	
	%CollisionShape2D1.position = Vector2(0, view.y / 2 )
	%CollisionShape2D2.position = Vector2(0, -view.y / 2 )

	%CollisionShape2D3.position = Vector2(-view.x / 2 , 0 )
	%CollisionShape2D4.position = Vector2(view.x / 2 , 0 )
```

The fix here is largely the same, meaning you need to not change the transform (i.e. `MailInventory.position`) continuously in `_process`.

So the proper fix is to either:

1. Move `position = view / 2` to `_ready` (and maybe also run it at `Viewport.size_changed`).
2. Move `position = view / 2` to `_physics_process`, although I would not recommend this, since you may end up fighting the physics engine in weird ways that aren't immediately apparent.
3. Enable the `top_level` property for `physical_letter` and `physical_letter2` at some point early in the program flow, which will prevent the rigid bodies from being affected by changes to their parent transform.

---

From looking at this a bit closer, it seems this worked prior to 4.7 due to what is either a `CanvasItem` bug, or an overly aggressive optimization.

Take this equivalent 3D script for example:

```gdscript
extends RigidBody3D

func _process(_delta: float) -> void:
	position = position
```

This script should (and have for a long time) result in the `RigidBody3D` freezing in-place, because of the following engine loop flow:

- Physics processing starts (if needed)
    - Run `_integrate_forces`
    - Fetch the latest data from the physics engine
    - Run `_physics_process`
    - Step the physics engine
    - Repeat (if needed)
- Idle processing starts
    - Run `_process`
    - Input, rendering, whatever else
- Repeat

As you can hopefully see there, `_process` will run **after** the physics engine has been stepped, but **before** we've had a chance to fetch that new data, which means that `position = position` will take the old yet-to-be-updated transform and send it to the physics server again, overwriting whatever the physics engine calculated, leading to the effect of the body freezing in-place.

In fact, this 2D script behaves as the 3D one, and did prior to 4.7 as well:

```gdscript
extends RigidBody2D

func _process(_delta: float) -> void:
	global_position = global_position
```

But for whatever reason this 2D script just happened to "work" prior to 4.7, meaning the body does not freeze in-place:

```gdscript
extends RigidBody2D

func _process(_delta: float) -> void:
	position = position
```

... because the setting of `position` there doesn't result in any `NOTIFICATION_TRANSFORM_CHANGED`, due to it ending up in [this early-out](https://github.com/godotengine/godot/blob/4b80850721c4f8d3f412d381d97e469c28b99482/scene/main/canvas_item.cpp#L1168) in `CanvasItem::_notify_transform`, due to `RigidBody2D::_sync_body_state` having set the `global_invalid` flag but then blocked the actual adding to `xform_change_list` using `block_transform_notify`, which means nothing ever gets sent to the physics server.

However, it seems one way to prevent that early-out from happening is to simply read from any part of the global transform before changing `position`, so this script behaves as I described even prior to 4.7:

```gdscript
extends RigidBody2D

func _process(_delta: float) -> void:
	print(global_position) # Just reading the global transform will lead to a different outcome
	position = position
```

Needless to say I don't think it's the right move to revert #118080 just to restore this seemingly fragile behavior. It's unfortunate that people seem to be relying on it though.

The real bug here is rather that `_set_global_invalid(true)` is called [here](https://github.com/godotengine/godot/blob/4b80850721c4f8d3f412d381d97e469c28b99482/scene/main/canvas_item.cpp#L1171) even when `block_transform_notify` is enabled (which is only the case in `RigidBody2D::_sync_body_state`) thus preventing explicit transform changes from propagating correctly. Fixing it won't really change anything as far as this issue (nor #121038) is concerned though.

@mihe's explanation makes perfect sense. Of course, I forgot the viewport is just a node and physicsbodies don't like when you move their parents much. I must have forgot because, well, everything just worked out of the box when i threw together the proof of concept for that part of my game.

If I can give my humble opinion as someone with zero knowledge of the engine's internal workings, my biggest issue was that I wasn't even aware this behaviour i was "relying" on was anything out of the ordinary, even after extensive research trying to find out what I did wrong between my code working and not working (before I realized the only change was an engine update).
Maybe throwing a warning when a similar situation happens, similar to how the engine tells you not to change the scale of collision shapes?

But thanks again for the insight and the suggestions on how to fix my code! 


P.S.
How come moving the window "unstuck" the rigid bodies?

> What was wrong with this commented out `p_node->xform_change.in_list() &&`? It looks like it fixes the canvas_item bug you mentioned.

I'm not sure. The change comes from [this commit](https://github.com/godotengine/godot/commit/da11d6d9e868db674cb18ced0544c84e3356be8d), which dates back to Godot 3.0 pre-alpha, titled "Many fixes to make exported scenes work better".

To my surprise it seems I had made a different attempt at fixing this issue once before (#84856, reverted in #84914) and had completely forgot about it. Even reading it now I have no recollection of doing this. Either way, I'd be hesitant about changing any of this stuff myself, due to risk of regressions elsewhere.

> Maybe throwing a warning when a similar situation happens, similar to how the engine tells you not to change the scale of collision shapes?

Yeah, something like this might be warranted, but I'm not sure what the heuristic should be for it. Just throwing a warning whenever you change a physics-related transform (directly or indirectly) from `_process` is likely going to yield a lot of noise and false positives. It's still somewhat reasonable to do one-off teleports from outside of physics processing. Maybe something that checks to see if it happens continuously over multiple process frames perhaps, but I wouldn't be surprised if that also causes friction for some.

> How come moving the window "unstuck" the rigid bodies?

I'm just guessing here, but dragging the window may have stalled the main loop (or at least idle processing) enough for multiple physics frames to run during during a single engine iteration, preventing `_process` from doing its overwriting.

Regarding the warning, I've noticed another unintended effect that might help notice something's wrong. After moving the rigidbody with `position = ...` the body "visually" sticks to the shelf, while a "ghost" of the rigidbody can be seen falling to the floor as the collision points become visible when they contact the floor. The invisible shape on the floor correctly responds to physics inputs from other bodies or being dragged by the joint. The debug visual for the collision shape also remains fixed in place in the shelf. Perhaps it's possible to check if the body is colliding outside of it's bounds, or if the visual and logical representations of a collision area are consistently in different places. I doubt that's ever intended, but obviously I have a lot less experience on what people might be doing in their projects. https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/2e46a996-1191-478c-a590-5a63169d7719
